clinician.final_diagnosis: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) secondary to COVID-19 infection
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension, fibromyalgia, and previous lumbar spinal fusion presented with sudden onset severe occipital headache, nausea, and mild photophobia 5 days after testing positive for COVID-19 via nasopharyngeal PCR. On admission, she was afebrile with normal oxygen saturations. Initial full blood count showed borderline-low platelets at 153×10⁹/L (normal range 140-400), mild leukopenia (WBC 3.4×10⁹/L), and lymphopenia (lymphocytes 0.7×10⁹/L). CT brain and chest X-ray were unremarkable. Three days after admission, while clinically stable with mild COVID-19 symptoms, repeat blood tests revealed acute marked thrombocytopenia with platelets dropping to 5×10⁹/L. Blood film confirmed true thrombocytopenia with no schistocytes, ruling out microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Comprehensive investigations including coagulation screen, rheumatological markers, viral panel (hepatitis B, C, HIV, CMV, EBV), haematinics, thyroid function, and H. pylori antigen were all unremarkable. The hematology team concluded that the acute reduction in platelet counts was most likely due to ITP secondary to COVID-19 infection. The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg for 2 days. After 1 day of IVIG, platelets improved to 10×10⁹/L. No platelet transfusion was given as the patient had no bleeding and CT brain was normal. At follow-up the day after discharge, platelets had increased to 41×10⁹/L. Headaches persisted throughout admission (intermittent to severe, frontal headaches) and were managed conservatively with analgesia per neurology recommendation. final.final_diagnosis: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) secondary to COVID-19 infection
final.trajectory_summary: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension, fibromyalgia, and previous lumbar spinal fusion presented with sudden onset severe occipital headache, nausea, and mild photophobia 5 days after testing positive for COVID-19 via nasopharyngeal PCR. On admission, she was afebrile with normal oxygen saturations. Initial full blood count showed borderline-low platelets at 153×10⁹/L (normal range 140-400), mild leukopenia (WBC 3.4×10⁹/L), and lymphopenia (lymphocytes 0.7×10⁹/L). CT brain and chest X-ray were unremarkable. Three days after admission, while clinically stable with mild COVID-19 symptoms, repeat blood tests revealed acute marked thrombocytopenia with platelets dropping to 5×10⁹/L. Blood film confirmed true thrombocytopenia with no schistocytes, ruling out microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Comprehensive investigations including coagulation screen, rheumatological markers, viral panel (hepatitis B, C, HIV, CMV, EBV), haematinics, thyroid function, and H. pylori antigen were all unremarkable. The hematology team concluded that the acute reduction in platelet counts was most likely due to ITP secondary to COVID-19 infection. The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg for 2 days. After 1 day of IVIG, platelets improved to 10×10⁹/L. No platelet transfusion was given as the patient had no bleeding and CT brain was normal. At follow-up the day after discharge, platelets had increased to 41×10⁹/L. Headaches persisted throughout admission (intermittent to severe, frontal headaches) and were managed conservatively with analgesia per neurology recommendation. The patient continued to have mild COVID-19 symptoms (shortness of breath on exertion and cough) but no fevers or oxygen requirement.
